cues.text: The Return to Rome
In 1377, Pope Gregory XI ended nearly seventy years of the Avignon Papacy by returning the papal see to Rome, dying there the following March.
His death left the Sacred College of Cardinals to elect a successor amid a restive Roman populace demanding, sometimes violently, an Italian or at least a Roman pope after decades of French pontiffs.
The Contested Election of Urban VI
On April 8, 1378, the cardinals elected the Neapolitan Archbishop of Bari, Bartolomeo Prignano , who took the name Urban VI .
A capable administrator, Urban proved harshly temperamental and reform-minded once enthroned, quickly alienating the same cardinals who had chosen him by attacking their luxury and privileges.
Fondi and the Election of Clement VII
Citing Rome's summer heat, the disaffected cardinals withdrew first to Anagni and then to Fondi , under Queen Joanna of Naples's protection.
There, thirteen declared Urban's election invalid — alleging it had been made under mob duress — and on September 20, 1378, elected Robert of Geneva as a rival pope, who took the name Clement VII .
Driven soon after from Naples, Clement withdrew to Avignon, and the schism was complete.
A Divided Christendom

Unlike earlier schisms caused by rival factions each backing a different candidate, this schism arose from a single body of cardinals repudiating their own choice — a fact that made the competing claims of legitimacy exceptionally difficult to adjudicate.

European kingdoms split their allegiance largely along political lines: France, Scotland, Castile, and Aragon recognized the Avignon line, while England, most of the Holy Roman Empire, and much of Italy backed the Roman popes.
Three Popes and the Path to Resolution
The schism outlived both original claimants, passing through successors on each side: Boniface IX, Innocent VII, and Gregory XII at Rome; Benedict XIII at Avignon.
A failed attempt at resolution by the Council of Pisa in 1409 only added a third papal line.
The schism was finally resolved by the Council of Constance (1414–1418), which secured the resignation or deposition of the rival claimants and elected Pope Martin V in 1417.
Legacy
The Western Schism did lasting damage to papal prestige and gave powerful impetus to the conciliarist movement.
This movement argued that a general council held authority even over the pope—a theory the Church would spend much of the following century working through.
The trauma of nearly forty years of division also fed reform pressures that would resurface, more explosively, in the Protestant Reformation of the following century.
